_README: Seed research question bank. 15 questions across four domains.
Each question carries a `factual_checklist`: the essential claims a correct
explanation should contain. These were written by the project authors and are
marked reviewed_by 'project author (initial pass)' — they are a starting point
for a domain reviewer, not a validated answer key.
`conceptual_difficulty` is an explicit field because the brief warns against
assuming all questions have equally difficult conceptual structure. Questions
differ in how many interacting parts a correct mental model needs.

questions.text: How does Redis caching reduce database load?
factual_checklist: A cache stores the result of an expensive operation so it can be reused.
A cache hit avoids querying the database entirely; a miss does not.
Reduction in load comes from fewer queries reaching the database, not from faster queries.
Cached copies can become stale when the underlying data changes.
Invalidation or expiry is required to manage staleness.
The benefit depends on repeated reads of the same data; unique requests gain nothing.

questions.text: What happens when a browser sends an HTTPS request?
factual_checklist: DNS resolution maps the hostname to an IP address.
A TCP connection is established before any TLS exchange.
A TLS handshake negotiates protocol version and cipher suite.
The server presents a certificate which the client validates against a trust chain.
Key exchange establishes symmetric session keys; bulk data uses symmetric encryption.
The HTTP request is sent inside the encrypted channel.
Encryption protects confidentiality and integrity in transit, not data at rest on either end.

questions.text: How does a database transaction maintain consistency?
factual_checklist: A transaction groups operations so they succeed or fail as a unit (atomicity).
Consistency means the database moves between states that satisfy its declared constraints.
Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe of each other.
Durability means a committed transaction survives failure.
Rollback undoes a partial transaction, usually via a write-ahead log or undo information.
Isolation levels trade correctness guarantees against concurrency.
Consistency in ACID is not the same as consistency in CAP.

questions.text: Why does a race condition occur?
factual_checklist: Two or more operations access shared mutable state concurrently.
At least one operation writes to that state.
The outcome depends on the relative timing of the operations.
Non-atomic read-modify-write sequences are a common cause.
The bug is often intermittent because timing varies between runs.
Mutual exclusion, atomic operations, or removing shared mutability prevent it.

questions.text: How does a message queue improve reliability?
factual_checklist: A queue decouples the producer from the consumer in time.
Work is persisted so it survives a consumer being unavailable.
The producer does not block on the consumer completing the work.
Retries become possible because the message remains available until acknowledged.
Queues absorb bursts, smoothing load on the consumer.
Delivery is typically at-least-once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.
A queue adds latency and operational complexity; it is a trade-off, not a free gain.
Source documents are split into chunks and embedded into vectors ahead of time.
A query is embedded using the same embedding model.
Retrieval finds chunks whose vectors are nearest to the query vector.
Retrieved text is inserted into the model's prompt as context.
The model generates an answer conditioned on that retrieved context.
Model weights are not updated; this is not fine-tuning.
Answer quality is bounded by retrieval quality: irrelevant retrieval yields a poor answer.

questions.text: Why are embeddings useful for semantic search?
factual_checklist: An embedding maps text to a point in a high-dimensional vector space.
Texts with similar meaning are placed close together in that space.
Similarity is computed geometrically, commonly by cosine similarity.
This matches meaning rather than shared keywords, so paraphrases can match.
Query and documents must be embedded by the same model for distances to be meaningful.
Embeddings capture the training distribution's notion of similarity, which may not match the user's.

questions.text: How does gradient descent update model parameters?
factual_checklist: A loss function measures how wrong the model's predictions are.
The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter.
The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase in loss.
Parameters are updated in the opposite direction of the gradient.
The learning rate scales the size of each step.
The process repeats over many batches of data.
Too large a learning rate can diverge; too small converges slowly.

questions.text: What is the difference between training and inference?
factual_checklist: Training adjusts model parameters using labelled or self-supervised data.
Inference uses fixed parameters to produce an output for new input.
Training requires computing gradients and a backward pass; inference does not.
Training is typically done once or periodically; inference runs per request.
Inference is usually far cheaper per example than training.
A model does not learn from the inputs it sees at inference time unless explicitly retrained.

questions.text: Why can a large language model hallucinate?
factual_checklist: The model is trained to produce likely continuations, not to verify truth.
It has no built-in mechanism to check a claim against an external source.
Plausible-sounding text and true text are not distinguished by the training objective.
Gaps or errors in training data can be reproduced or interpolated over.
Specific details such as names, numbers and citations are especially prone to fabrication.
Fluency is not evidence of accuracy.
Retrieval or tool use can reduce but does not eliminate the problem.

questions.text: Why is a p-value not the probability that a hypothesis is true?
factual_checklist: A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
It is a conditional probability of data given a hypothesis, not of a hypothesis given data.
Transposing that conditional is a logical error.
Obtaining the probability of a hypothesis requires a prior and Bayes' theorem.
A small p-value does not quantify effect size or practical importance.
A large p-value is not evidence that the null hypothesis is true.

questions.text: How does gradient descent find a minimum?
factual_checklist: It follows the local downhill direction given by the negative gradient.
It is a local method: it uses no information about the global shape of the surface.
It converges to a point where the gradient is approximately zero (a stationary point).
A stationary point may be a local minimum, a saddle point, or a plateau.
Convexity guarantees a local minimum is global; most interesting problems are non-convex.
Step size determines whether it converges, oscillates, or diverges.

questions.text: Why does correlation not establish causation?
factual_checklist: Correlation measures statistical association between two variables.
An association is consistent with several causal structures.
A third variable can cause both (confounding).
The causal direction may be the reverse of the one assumed.
Selection effects and sampling can create association without causation.
Coincidence can produce association, especially with many comparisons.
Randomised assignment or explicit causal assumptions are needed to support a causal claim.
Satellites broadcast signals containing a precise transmission timestamp and their own position.
The receiver measures signal travel time to compute distance to each satellite.
Distance to one satellite places the receiver on a sphere; intersecting spheres narrow the position.
Three satellites would suffice with a perfect clock; a fourth is needed to solve for receiver clock error.
The receiver solves for four unknowns: three position coordinates and a time offset.
Accuracy is limited by atmospheric delay, signal reflection, and satellite geometry.
The receiver only listens; it does not transmit to the satellites.

questions.text: Why does a refrigerator move heat from inside to outside?
factual_checklist: Heat flows spontaneously only from hotter to colder, so moving it the other way requires work.
A refrigerant cycles between liquid and gas phases.
Evaporating refrigerant absorbs heat from inside the cabinet.
A compressor does work on the refrigerant, raising its pressure and temperature.
The refrigerant then condenses outside, releasing heat to the warmer room.
An expansion valve drops the pressure so the refrigerant can evaporate cold again.
A refrigerator moves heat; it does not destroy it, so the room net warms.
